newsitem.title: USA: Boeing denies plans for futuristic superjumbo.
newsitem.headline: Boeing denies plans for futuristic superjumbo.

text.p: Boeing Co. Friday denied reports suggesting that it had shelved plans to produce a bigger version of its 747 jumbo jet to concentrate on developing a futuristic superjumbo with twice the capacity.

Reports in both The Times and The Independent newspapers in Britain speculated Boeing had decided to focus instead on a futuristic 800-seat "giant flying wing" concept being developed by Boeing's prospective acquisition McDonnell Douglas Corp.
"As much as we know about that program is what we've read in the papers," said Boeing spokesman in Chris Villiers. "The decision (to shelve the 747-X) was strictly a business case decision."

McDonnell Douglas is in the final year of a $3 million NASA research contract to study the so-called blended wing-body airliner, which would have a shape resembling the triangular B-2 stealth bomber and better aerodynamic efficiency than conventional commercial jets.
A remote control model with a 17-foot wingspan is being built at Stanford University and scheduled to take its first flight sometime in the spring.
Officials at NASA and McDonnell Douglas said the project is in the very earliest stages of research, noting that $3 million is a minuscule amount for an aerospace project.
"It's going on at a relatively low level because we have an interest in this technology," said Keith Henry of the space agency's Langley Research Center in Hampton, Va.
He said the future of the study was uncertain in part because of Boeing's plan to acquire McDonnell Douglas in a $15 billion stock deal expected to be completed in the summer.

As envisioned the plane would be about 161 feet long with a basic wing span of 280 feet, making it too large to fit into standard airport jet bays designed to accommodate the 747, but it would be able to take off from standard airport runways.
By contrast the current 747 is 232 feet long with a wingspan of 211 feet.
Passengers in the "flying wing" would sit on two decks in seating that would extend into the wing area and feature very few windows, Henry said.

Published reports have suggested the giant-wing airplane could be put into commercial service by 2010 or before at a development cost of $20 billion, but McDonnell Douglas spokesman David Eastman said the study so far has focused only on technology.
"We don't even know if there's a market," he said.

Boeing said this week it had shelved its 747-X project because too few airlines wanted to commit themselves yet and projected costs had more than doubled to $7 billion because airlines wanted almost a wholly new plane rather than a stretched version of the existing 747.

But Boeing is keeping a close watch on the progress of arch rival Airbus Industrie's proposals to produce an A3XX double-decker aircraft by 2003 with initial seating capacity of 550 passengers, compared with about 415 for the 747.
And while Boeing is focusing on new versions of its medium-sized jets, the Seattle-based company is leaving a skeleton crew in place to continue working on the 747-X.
"If the market develops we will be ready," a Boeing spokesman said.
